rows.note: Arabic ءَامَنُوا۟ means they believed, and Hebrew אמן likewise means to believe or trust.

rows.explanation: Abram believes in the LORD, and that belief is reckoned to him as righteousness.
Israel believes in the LORD after seeing his deliverance.
The LORD asks how long the people will refuse to believe in him.
Jehoshaphat urges the people to believe in the LORD.
The people of Nineveh believe God.
Daniel is unharmed because he trusted in his God, using Biblical Aramaic אמן.

rows.note: Arabic وَعَمِلُوا۟ means they did deeds, while Hebrew עמל usually means laborious or wearying work.

rows.explanation: A person’s עמל is labor under the sun, with a more arduous sense than doing deeds.
The speaker surveys all the work for which he labored.
The builders labor in vain unless the LORD builds the house.
Job’s “nights of עמל” show the Hebrew word’s further sense of hardship.

rows.note: Arabic ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ describes righteous deeds, while Hebrew and Biblical Aramaic צלח chiefly mean to succeed or prosper.

rows.explanation: Joshua’s way will prosper, expressing success rather than the moral goodness of deeds.
The LORD’s purpose will prosper in his servant’s hand.
The builders prosper in their work, using the Biblical Aramaic cognate.
The spirit of the LORD rushes upon David, showing another Hebrew use distinct from righteous deeds.

rows.note: Arabic وَتَوَاصَوْا۟ means they exhorted one another, and no secure Biblical Hebrew or Aramaic cognate is identified here.
Arabic ٱلْحَقِّ means truth or what is right, while Hebrew חקק and its nouns concern prescribing statutes or fixed dues.

rows.explanation: Israel’s חקים are called righteous statutes, linking prescribed law with what is right.
The LORD commands Israel to keep his statutes, using the Hebrew legal sense.
The priests’ חק is their fixed allotment, a prescribed due rather than truth.

rows.note: Arabic ٱلصَّبْرِ means patience, whereas the sound-matched Hebrew צבר means to heap up and is not a secure cognate.
